en: Cāmuṇḍa (also known as Kāyastha, i.e., Kāyasthacāmuṇḍa, or simply Caṇḍa; circa 1490 CE):
*Rasasaṃketakalikā* (also known as *Rasasaṅketakalikā*).
Having bowed to Śiva, the Lord of Mercury (Raseśa), Cāmuṇḍa, born of the Kāyastha lineage,
composes this *Rasasaṃketakalikā*, which bestows the attainment of desired goals.
(Origin of Mercury’s Myth):
For the sake of slaying Tāraka, the gods held [the seed] on Kailāsa that had issued from Śambhu during his dalliance with Rati;
it was then taken into the mouth by Agni.
He cast it separately in each of the four directions into the salt ocean;
that which was situated in the three directions beginning with the north did not accomplish its purpose due to the curse of Gaurī.
In the west, that [planet] is liberated; it becomes the charioteer (Mercury), the performer of all tasks.
White, reddish, turmeric-colored, and black are the wives of the Brahmins and the other [castes], ending with the Pāradas.
The impurities of mercury (rasadoṣas) should be applied to the body, iron, or lead, or else to their respective types; in these,
there are five natural defects and seven coatings (kañcukas).

The five defects, beginning with impurity (mala), and the seven coverings (kañcuka), beginning with earth (bhū), reside within the vital essence (rasa) and produce the twelve [diseases], beginning with leprosy (kuṣṭha). Rsk_1.6.

(18 Saṃskāras) Therefore, eighteen purificatory rites have been taught by the wise for the sake of liberation from defects; since they are difficult to perform, they are declared to be easy to perform through the *rasa* [of mercury]. Rsk_1.7 //
Mercury (the quicksilver): from one *pala* up to fifty *palas* is the correct weight for mercury;
less or more than that, the mercury should not be processed by the wise.
On an auspicious day, the purified mercury should be placed within a fourfold cloth and kept aside; then,
one should rub it in a mortar made of iron, copper, or stone while it is heated.
Mercury, rubbed for one day with brick-dust, *asurī*, soot, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), sour substances, and salts, each taken in a portion equal to its time (i.e., one part), becomes purified.
Then, covered with cloth, it should be subjected to sudation for a day using alkaline substances, acids, urine,
and so forth.
One should then perform the *mūrcchanā* seven times with the [substances] known as *kanyā*, fire, sun, and excellent water.
By precipitating it three times with the upward-precipitation method (*ūrdhvapātana*), mercury extracted from cinnabar (*hiṅgulākṛṣṭa*) becomes pure when combined with one-fourth part of iron.
Or mercury extracted from cinnabar may indeed be free from defects.
The dull-witted person who, having abandoned the Guru’s scripture, attempts to produce mercury without sulphur that has been subjected to *jāraṇa*, shall be cursed by the Lord of Mercury.
The mercury and sulphur, one part each, should be ground little by little in a mortar;
through repeated pounding, it becomes a paste, or else it is placed in a copper vessel.
Having added an equal amount of sulfur and sealed it within an iron crucible,
one should cook it in a *bhūdhara* furnace until the sulfur is fully digested.
In this manner, the fragrant powder should be administered again and again until it has increased sixfold;
when the fragrance has been digested sixfold, the mercury becomes a destroyer of all diseases.
The *pāṭa*, the *khoṭa*, the *jalaukā*, and the fourth, called *bhasma*—
these four types of binding (*bandha*) of mercury are to be understood by the best of physicians. (Rsk 1.17)
*Pāṭa* is the *parpaṭikā*-bond; *piṣṭibandha*, however, is the *khoṭaka*. *Jalaukā* is the *pakvabandha*; *bhasma* becomes like ashes. (Rsk 1.18)
Mercurial ash (sūtabhasma) is to be known as twofold: that which moves upward (ūrdhvaga) and that which remains at the bottom (talabhasma).
Listen to the description of the *sthālikā-sampuṭa* apparatus, which produces the *ūrdhvabhasma*. (Rsk 1.19)
The ritual procedure involves two pots in the center, each sixteen finger-breadths on all sides;
having filled the lower pot with slightly moistened salt, [one should proceed].
One should smear the joints with clay and enclose [the vessel] with another [layer];
having placed it upon a three-doored furnace, one should maintain a steady fire for four watches (yāmas).
One should cook it until it is cooled by its own heat; then, having removed it, one should discard the salt.
Having placed the saline [substance] at the top, the Lord of Tastes (mercury) should be cast into another [liquid].
Having encased it as before, one should then place it in a basin;
having made the trench firm, one should pour water into it.
Having repeatedly discarded the hot [ashes], one should repeatedly throw in cold ones;
at each of the three doors, one should insert a single long piece of wood measuring one cubit.
The wise one should first ignite a mass of fuel the size of a handful;
above that, he should place two pieces of wood, and above those, he should insert a triad.
After two watches (yāma), one should discard the charcoal and the water;
that which remains adhered to the upper vessel is the ash above, which bestows accomplishment (siddhi).
Take equal parts of each of these three: sulfur, the essence of soot, and purified mercury.
One should grind it for one watch (yāma) in a mortar and place it inside a glass flask.
Having sealed it for twelve yāmas, one should cook it in a sand-bath (vālukāyantra);
once it has cooled of its own accord, one should break it open and discard the sulphur from above.
Cinnabar ash is a vehicle for medicinal formulations and is the remover of all diseases.
I shall now describe the change of color resulting from the combination with other medicinal substances.
Red, yellow, black, blue, pale white, and reddish-brown—
[these are] combined with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and mixed with mercury (*capala*). Rsk_1.30.
The ash shall be red in color, resembling the flower of the pomegranate (*dāḍima*).
[For yellow ash:
one should grind the juice and the fragrance of *bhūdhātrī* and *hastiśuṇḍī*.
The mercury, processed for four watches in a glass vessel and mixed with black ash,
combined with sulfur, and rubbed with the juice of kumārī, should be drunk. (Rasakalpa 1.32)
The ash should be black in color, difficult to obtain even for the gods;
it should be combined with the *vārāhī* tuber and accompanied by mercury.
Ash that is dark-colored destroys wrinkles and graying hair;
ash that is pale-red occurs in a small jar smeared with salt.
Twenty parts of salt and one part of mercury,
having been rubbed together in sour gruel (*kāñjika*), shall attain the state of ash through heating in a *puṭa* on the fire. (Rasārṇava 1.35)
Having extracted another [base] essence and added it as desired, one should kill the mercury;
in this way, copper, lead, tin, and mica, when killed, become providers of [alchemical] qualities.
Having placed that [substance] slowly in a vessel filled with water for eight watches (yāmas),
one should discard the water and take the essence remaining in the vessel, which is the mercury in the form of ash.
One should prepare two crucibles with the powder of *apāmārga* seeds;
having placed mercury inside them and rubbed it with *malayū* juice, one should subject it to *puṭa* firing.
Having placed the powder of *droṇapuṣpī* flowers, *viḍaṅga*,
and *arimedaka* both below and above, one should apply the seal (*mudrā*).
Having properly prepared the *golaka* (pill), one should place it inside a pair of earthen crucibles (*mṛnmūṣā-sampuṭa*);
having sealed it and dried it, one should then cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
In this manner, mercury attains the state of ash with a single *puṭa* application;
having removed it while still cool to the touch, one should employ it in all ritual operations.
One should place [the mercury] in a shallow pan on the hearth smeared with crystal;
having been cooked in the juice of *punarnavā*, the mercury dies through the process of rubbing.
(Examination of Mercury:: Death) When mercury is lusterless, heavy, white, corrosive to iron, and immobile;
when it does not circulate in fire nor rise upwards, then it is dead. (Rsk 1.43)
Mercury destroys all diseases, acts as a vehicle for other substances, is laxative, and is heavy.
It cures pallor, worms, and leprosy; it is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and a rejuvenative elixir.
All metallic essences, when repeatedly processed, become increasingly superior in their qualities.
One should preserve the prepared mercury by storing it in a tooth, a horn, a gem, or a bamboo tube.
(Regarding the weight of the drugs:
for poisons, one sixteenth part of a *pitta* is a *raktikā*.
Even when not explicitly stated, this rule should be understood to apply automatically to pills (*guṭī*) and liquid extracts (*rasa*). (Rsk 1.46)

For the purpose of destroying all diseases and for the sake of strengthening the body, one who has purified the body, eats wholesome food, and worships the worshipful [deity] should practice the consumption [of mercury]. (Rasendrakalpa 1.47)
One *vallaka* for a man, one *gadyāṇa* for a horse, and two for an elephant;
the physician who administers these, or the one who treats with his own medicines using the two types of minerals, shall remove diseases.
When there is a disorder of the rasa (plasma), fainting, hiccup, fever,
restlessness, cough, dyspnea, giddiness, delusion, burning sensation, and trembling arise.
For its pacification, one should drink the juice of a citron (*bījapūra*), ginger, and rock salt;
or one should drink the auspicious root of the *karkoṭaka* plant prepared in cow’s urine.
In that house where the Lord of Tastes (Venus) is worshipped with great devotion,
it shall be filled with offspring and wealth, and be free from mental anguish and physical disease.
Gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron— these are declared to be the six metals (*ṣaḍloha*).
(Artificial metals)
These, such as Ghoṣāvartaka and others, are natural; however, those [others] are artificial.
Pure, dead, and reconstituted [metals] are traditionally held to cure all diseases.
One should discard impure metals and those that have undergone insufficient processing, as they bestow disease and death.
Metal joined with mercury abandons its defects, and mercury likewise [abandons its defects] when joined with metal.
Therefore, one should not kill metals such as gold and the like without mercury.
Gold is said to be of five kinds: natural (*prākṛta*), born from fire (*sahajāgnija*),
and this triad of gold is fit for the consumption of the gods, possessing sixteen color-grades (*varṇa*).
Mineral [mercury] produced from the science of alchemy (rasavāda), having been purified and processed into excellent leaves,
enriched with fourteen medicinal substances, is fit for human use and destroys disease.
Gold becomes pure when immersed seven times in the juice of the *kāñcanāra* tree.
(Gold:: Killing)
When the gold has been melted, one should cast in a serpent [of mercury] weighing one-sixteenth part.
Having rubbed it with acid and formed a ball from it,
one should place sulfur equal in amount to the ball both below and above it.
Having placed [the substance] in a pair of earthen bowls and sealed them, one should heat it over a fire of thirty forest lotuses; after seven such cycles, it will turn to ash.
Gold is bitter and astringent, it removes fever, is sweet in its post-digestive effect, and bestows strength.
It bestows vitality and beauty, is aphrodisiac, and removes consumption, misfortune, and poison.
Silver is of three types: *sahaja* (naturally occurring) on Mount Kailāsa, *khanija* (mineral-derived) from the earth, and *kṛtrima* (artificial).
In terms of their qualities, they are best when listed in reverse order; that which is extracted from lead is beneficial for alchemical processing (*rasa*).
Silver is purified by the juice of white *agasti* in the same manner as gold;
its killing [is performed] likewise.
Having removed lead by means of the combination of sulphur and sour gruel, one should cast in tin.
It promotes youth, semen, strength, and energy, and removes all diseases.
When a sword smeared with this ash and acid becomes copper-colored, then death [is imminent].
If neither gold nor silver is present in the yoga,
then iron produced from magnetite (kāntaloha) should be added there, possessing qualities equal to those [of the other two].
There are two types of copper: Nepalese and barbarian; among these, the Nepalese is superior in its metallic essence.
As for the physical properties of Nepalese copper:
It withstands heavy blows, is glossy, has red petals, is stainless, and is soft.
The *mleccha* [iron], however, when washed, is black, rough, rigid, and unable to withstand being forged;
mixed with *nāga* and copper, it is not excellent for alchemical work (*rasakarma*).
Copper should be known as being like poison; indeed, it must be processed with great care.
There is one defect in poison, whereas eight are proclaimed in copper. (Rsk 2.16)
Leucoderma, purgation, vomiting, vertigo, fever, wind-disorder, jaundice, and the destruction of the body—these eight defects have been described by the wise. (Rsk 2.17)
One should boil a copper leaf over a steady fire for one day with cow urine;
thereafter, it should be washed with water twenty-one times to become pure. (Rasakalpa 2.18)
One should grind mercury, sulfur, and copper in equal parts with acid;
from this, ash is produced using either the *tripuṭa* crucible or the *vālukāyantra*. (Rasakalpa 2.19)
Take two parts of sulfur and one part of copper, place them in a sealed crucible made of two earthenware bowls (*śarāva*), and roast them.
Once they have cooled naturally, grind them together in a mortar and strain the mixture through a cloth.
Having made that equal to sea salt, one should perform the sealing again;
when that is exhausted, one should add more of that very same sea salt, repeatedly.
One should repeatedly saturate it with the water of green vitriol;
thus, through sixty-four saturations, it becomes "niruttha," fit for application in yoga.
That copper should be sealed within a *sauraṇa* tuber or in *pañcāmṛta*;
it does not produce the eight previously mentioned defects and brings about beneficial qualities.
It destroys Gulma, consumption, indigestion, cough, anemia, and fever;
it cures obesity, abdominal enlargement, and Kapha-related pain, and is a supreme purifier for both the upper and lower tracts.
Tin is said to be of two types: *khuraka* and *miśraka*.
Of these, *khuraka* is superior in its qualities, whereas *miśraka* is not beneficial for the taste.
(Tin:: Purification) Tin and lead are to be purified twenty-one times in the juice of *kanyā* and *bhṛṅga*,
or else in a decoction of *brahmavṛkṣa* or *nirguṇḍī*.
In a clay vessel containing molten tin, one should throw the powder of the bark of the tamarind and the holy fig tree;
adding a fourth part of that [to the mixture], one should stir it with an iron ladle.
Once it has been reduced to ashes,
one should then grind it with one tāla of realgar using a paste and decoction of *brahmadru* (khadira), and cook it in a *gajapuṭa*.
Having added one-tenth part [of mercury] in each layer, one should thus layer it ten times;
that lead-ash, being "niruttha," cures the disease of pāṇḍu-meha.
A leaf of tin placed within a hollow of dried cow-dung and combined with goat dung dies by merely being subjected to the *puṭapāka* process; it destroys twenty types of urinary disorders (*meha*).
First, having prepared the ash of tin and lead along with an equal amount of mica,
one should grind them with rice-husk water and then apply a *gajapuṭa* firing.
Having added one-sixtieth part of sulfur, it should be cooked for up to sixty puṭas;
that lead ash is "niruttha" (non-reactive) and possesses qualities superior to those of tin ash.
Lead, tin, and silver are equal in their qualities to the ash of mercury (*rasabhasma*).
And when they cannot be obtained for one another, one should join them with each other.
Munda, tikshna, and likewise kānta; its subdivisions are thirteen.
(Subdivisions of Munda)
The *muṇḍa* is said to be of three kinds: soft, blunt, and having a protruding shaft.
(The subtypes of sharp iron:
Kharasāra, hotrāsa, tārāvarta, and likewise viḍa.
Kānta, loha, and that called gaja—thus the sixfold *tīkṣṇa* (steel) is described.

(Examination of Magnetic Iron): That iron which is called *kānta* is characterized by these signs and none other: when it is placed in water, a drop of oil does not spread upon it; asafoetida does not release its own scent; the paste of neem does not impart its bitterness; when cooked, milk takes on the shape of a peak; and it does not sink into the ground. Rsk_2.36.
Loha is said to be of four types: kānta, romaka, bhrāmaka, and likewise cumbaka and drāvaka; its qualities increase progressively in each subsequent one.
The wise one should purify all metals, such as iron and others, in the same manner as copper.
(Iron:: Pāka)
The smelting of metals is said to be threefold: mild, middling, and hard;
the first two are like mud and dry clay, while the hard is like sand.
An iron leaf smeared with the fragrance [of the medicine], heated repeatedly in fire,
should be cast into the juice of *mīnākṣikā* until it dissolves right there.

One should grind that [mercury] firmly with an equal amount of mercury, cinnabar, and sulfur, using the milks of *nirguṇḍī*, *vṛṣa*, and *matsyākṣī*; death [of the mercury] occurs through *gajapuṭa* firing.
Having repeatedly formed a bolus of iron powder in a decoction of *varā*, [one should proceed with] the water-based killing of iron.
Indeed, one should perform the puṭapāka in a windless pit measuring sixteen finger-breadths.
By means of exactly sixty-four folds, it becomes like a ruby;
when it is free from water and rises up, it becomes a "yogavāhin" [substance] that removes all diseases.
In a decoction of rose-apple bark, or in a decoction of *tinduka* or *mārkaṇḍa* leaves; or in *vāritara*.
Having dried it twenty-one times, it should be ground and made into a liquid extract with water.
(Iron:: Killing) One should place an iron leaf resembling a tamarind leaf into the juice of *dantī*;
having kept it in the heat, the liquid should be administered until that [iron] becomes dead.
One should place an iron leaf into the midst of fish-eyes and milk.
During the summer heat, however, it should be changed every thirty days.
If silver,
having been processed with iron, honey, and clarified butter, is smelted, it returns to its original weight.
Then the iron becomes "without residue" (niruttha); otherwise, one should refine it again.
When the decoction of *varā* has been reduced to one-quarter, an equal amount of iron and clarified butter, along with sugar in a quantity equal to the iron,
should be cooked in a copper vessel; thus it becomes like nectar.
[Dead iron] cures disorders of the duodenum, anemia, edema, hemorrhoids, fever, abdominal tumors, and urinary disorders.
This iron medicine destroys diseases of the spleen and increases strength and intelligence.
One who serves iron should renounce the *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourd, sesame oil, food made of black gram (*māṣa*), mustard seeds, liquor, and sour juices.
Iron rust (*maṇḍūra*) should be purified by heating it seven times in cow’s urine and in a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
the dross (*kiṭṭa*) of all metals, such as gold and others, brings forth their respective qualities.
O Shaven-headed One, muṇḍa is ten times more potent than kiṭṭa; tīkṣṇa is more than a hundred times more potent than muṇḍa;
and kānta is a hundred thousand times more potent than tīkṣṇa. Through its consumption, it produces excellent qualities.
The essence produced from a crucible, contained within salt inside a vessel,
having been easily sealed and thoroughly cooked by the "elephant-fire" (*gajavahni*), that [essence] dies.
Dead mercury (mṛtarasaka), being dry, destroys the three doṣas and removes fever.
It cures diarrhea caused by the departure of *yoga*, destroys moisture, and causes constipation of the feces.
Regarding bell-metal and brass,
their purification and killing are said to be like those of copper.
White sugar mixed with cow’s milk should be administered in cases of abnormality caused by the consumption of minerals.
Now, one part of mercury and two parts of sulphur;
with these two in equal measure, gold and other metals that have not been rendered inert are quickly killed.

(Metals:: Residue:: Examination) When dead metals are smelted with equal parts of sal ammoniac, borax, guñjā, and molasses, and formed into a mass, they do not come back to life; these are called *niruttha* residues.
The element that has arisen with its scent should be ground for a day in the juice of a maiden.
When matured by the elephant-puta, everything becomes divine and free from impurities.
Yellow, white, black, and red—
each of these four types of sky-like clouds (*kha*) should be examined in the fire as *pināka*, *dardura*, *nāga*, and *vajra*.
One should not make leaves or sounds; that which is so characterized is known as "vajra" (thunderbolt).
When the three are smelted, the dross indeed leaves behind the essence, which is the Vajrin.
That essence should be taken according to the ritual procedure, purified, and killed like [the preparation of] metal.
But in the absence of *sattva*, it is said that when there is no moon (*niścandra*) among the flavors (*rasa*), that is what is intended.

Having thoroughly ground paddy-cloud (dhānyābhra) with peacock feathers, the tears from the eyes of a fish, *jambhala*, and borax in a mortar, one should then apply twelve "elephant-pots" (*gajapuṭa*) in this manner.

One should grind the mercury for seven nights with the juices of *mīnākṣī* and *bhṛṅga*, combined with water decocted from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). Then, having added an equal amount of sulfur, the mica (*abhra*) attains the state of quintuplication (*pañcatā*) through an excellent "elephant-seal" (*gajapuṭa*) firing.
Dead mica that has attained a moonless state is reddish and like nectar.
That which is accompanied by the moon should be known as like poison; it brings about death, like the hair of a tiger.
Excellently prepared water, cow’s ghee, and mica (abhraka), in proportions of one, six, and ten parts respectively,
should be cooked over a mild fire in an iron vessel; this constitutes the process of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).
It arrests the aging process, removes old age and death, maintains strength and health, and cures even great skin diseases.
Mṛta-meghaka, when employed against all diseases, is always equal in potency to the king of elixirs (sūtarāja).
Alkaline and sour substances, pulses, karkoṭika,
aravellaka, vṛntāka, and karīra, as well as oil, should be avoided during the practice of abhraka.
(Refining the Great Tastes: *Mahārasa-śodhana*) Gandhaka and Viṣadinepāla are purified in cow’s milk; likewise, Śilājatu [is purified] in cow’s urine.
Tālaka and the others are purified by cow’s urine, while Śaṅkha and the others become pure through acidic liquids.
Regarding the killing [of mercury], the poison mentioned among the liquids should be taken; it is to be ground with borax until equalized.
That [poison] becomes dead and "yogavāhi" (active in combination), possessing qualities equal to those of mercury, mica, and iron.
Poison consecrated seven times with the mantra known as Nīlakaṇṭha should be administered,
whether in the form of medicine or as a liquid extract, by one desiring the patient's welfare.
Those diseases here that are not cured by various medicinal substances and decoctions—
those arising from wind and phlegm perish quickly once the poison has been administered.
The superior, middling, and inferior doses consist of eight, six, and four barley-corns respectively.
When it has been consumed in an excessive dose, one should then drink clarified butter with potassium carbonate (ṭaṅkaṇa).
One should lick either *rajanī*, *meghanāda*, or *sarpākṣī* mixed with ghee,
or the powdered bark of the *arjuna* tree with honey and clarified butter.

It should not be given to one who is angry, nor to a weakling, nor to one afflicted by bile, nor to one suffering from pulmonary consumption; nor to one overcome by hunger, thirst, dizziness, heat, or travel, nor to one who is emaciated or diseased.

Poison should not be administered to pregnant women, children, or the elderly, nor within the royal palace; it may, however, be given to one devoted to elixirs who subsists on ghee, milk, and wholesome food.
Lāṅgalī, vajrī, hemārkā, hayāri, and viṣamuṣṭikā—
these they call minor poisons (upaviṣas), which are used in the process of mercury extraction (rasakarma).
While the ocean was being churned, [the ahiphena] flowed forth from the mouth of Vāsuki.
And due to its agitation, a flood of foam fell to the ground with a hissing sound.
Therefore it is called *ahiphena*; it is bitter, constipating, and desiccant.
It destroys delusion, difficult breathlessness, and cough; once practiced, one is unable to abandon it.
When prepared with skill, that [substance] which produces phlegm and wind is like nectar;
it causes the retention of semen in men and bestows pleasure upon women. (Rsk 3.12)
In ancient times, the ocean of jewels was churned by both the gods and the demons.
Therefore, the nectar that arose was drunk by the gods, not by the Dānavas.
Then, as the nectar fell from the hand of Dhanvantari onto the earth,
while it was being licked by all, his tongue was split in two by the *darbha* grass.
The great medicinal herb Siddhamūlī, produced from the blood and poison of the tongue,
is fourfold according to its flowers: white, red, yellow, and black.
Siddhamūlī,
whose form is joy, bestows success in yoga and mantra.
She is the remover of all diseases, the arouser of desire, and the awakener of hunger.
Now, some of the *rasas* that produce conviction will be described, as they have come down through tradition from the mouth of the Guru and from having studied the scriptures. (Rsk 4.1)
Mercury, *rasaka*, *tāla*, *tuttha*, sulfur,
and *ṭaṅkaṇa*— all these, purified and in equal parts, [should be macerated] for one day with the juices of *kāravelī*.
One should crush it and place it inside the thick interior of a copper vessel measuring half of a half-finger [in thickness]; that should then be cooked over two layers of sand.
While the grains are still bursting within the apparatus,
the wise should then extract [the substance] from the interior of a copper vessel once it has become thoroughly cooled.
Having added an equal amount of black pepper, one should grind everything together into a powder;
two *guñjā* seeds of this, taken with a piece of *parṇa* leaf, [cures] fever caused by wind (*vātika*) or bile (*paittika*).

One should administer one *guñjā* with sugar; in cases of *kapha*-dominant fever, three *guñjās* combined with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) are given; and in *saṃnipāta* fever, one *valla* should be given with the juice of fresh ginger.
This elixir named Śītabhañjī, created by Rudra, destroys irregular, acute fevers that recur every one, two, three, or four days.
Having ground mercury, sulfur, mica, and orpiment with the juices of *nimbū* fruits,
one should smear thin leaves of copper and place them in an apparatus called the "ash-pan."
One should heat [the mercury] for eight yāmas in fire and remove it once it has cooled to the touch of one's own body;
having added a fourth part of poison and pungent substances, pills the size of a *valla* are prepared.
The mercury known as Caitanyabhairava, bound with the juices of *devadālī* and administered with the juices of fresh ginger,
effects the destruction of all *saṃnipāta* fevers.
If a man has fallen to the ground unconscious, afflicted by cold, and exhausted, one should awaken him immediately; in the event of burning sensations, one should apply cooling treatments.
The five bile-substances—those of the boar, goat, fish, horse, and peacock—should be used;
having been consecrated with these, Caitanyabhairava should be administered.
Having placed one-sixteenth part of the mercury and poison inside a shallow bowl smeared with borax,
one should seal it and cook it on a slow fire over a hearth for two watches (six hours).
One should personally take the cooled [medicine] from the top of the bowl and,
avoiding the wind, pour it into a water-pot in the case of a combined fever or a snakebite.
It should be administered with the point of a needle, for a person awakens in an instant;
otherwise, one should administer it after the palate region has been scraped with a razor.
Mercury, sulfur, and Nepalese mica, increased in quantity and moistened with the juice of dantī,
taken for two watches along with one guñjā of sugar, destroy fever.
One should give two *ṭaṅkas* of *kṛṣṇa*, eight *ballakas* of *dhūrtabīja*, and three *pālikās* [of mercury]; this removes quartan fever.
At the time when the fever arrives, one should sprinkle the head with four jars of cold water and administer milk mixed with sugar as the wholesome diet.
Equal parts of nimba seeds, śilājājī, dhūma, and kṛṣṇā should be saturated twenty-one times with the juice of kāravelī.
If one applies [this] ointment to the eyes from the side, it conquers fever arising from that side;
this elixir named Ardhanārīnaṭeśa is a performer of wonders.
Cinnabar, black pepper, sulphur, long pepper, borax, poison,
and the seeds of *kanaka*— these in equal parts [are to be processed] with the juices of *vijayā*.
Having massaged it for just one *yāma*, a pill the size of a chickpea (*caṇa*) is prepared;
this "Gold-Beloved" (*Hemasundara*) destroys fever, dysentery, and chronic diarrhea (*grahaṇī*).
Having repeatedly rubbed one *pala* of purified mercury with the milky sap of the *arka* plant,
[one should add] two *palas* of purified sulfur and eight *palas* of great *kambu*.

Both [substances] should be processed with mercury for three days—subjected to heating, grinding, and drying—and then mixed with the previously prepared elixir; one should add half as much borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*).
Then, one should grind everything firmly with the milky sap of *arka* for one watch (three hours).
Once it is dry, having sealed it in a vessel smeared with powder, one should cook it in a *puṭa*.
One should eat four guñjās of it combined with black pepper and clarified butter;
as wholesome diet, curd-rice should be given, and at night, Vijayā mixed with jaggery.
For the purpose of destroying disorders of the *grahaṇī*, there is nothing equal to this on earth;
the mercury known as *arkalokeśvara* destroys all *grahaṇī* diseases.
One *tāla* of four-part stone (*catuḥśilā*) should be infused with the juices of the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*) for one day,
then ground with the juice of *vāsā* and cooked in a *vālukāyantra*.

At the end of two watches of the night, having extracted [the juice], one should add an equal amount of the three pungents (kaṭutraya) and the powder of nirguṇḍī root, combined with the juice of vāsā.
A single *guñjā* of this *śilātāleśvara* conquers asthma and cough;
[the ingredients are] mercury, the ash of gold and mica, realgar, sulfur, and *tālaka*.
Having thus made the individual earth-born [substances] each one by one into indivisible units (*aikākhya*),
he should fill the *varāṭī* shells with that [mixture] and with goat’s milk and *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Having ground [the ingredients] with that, one should block the mouth [of the vessel] and cook it in a shallow earthen dish or a pit in the ground;
once cooled to the touch of one's own body, one should remove it and strain it through a cloth.
This mercury, known as Rājamṛgāṅka, consists of four guñjās and removes consumption;
one should lick half a *valla* of gold and calcined mercury with honey.
One who eats wholesome food and observes celibacy becomes like the moon, which wards off waning;
likewise for one who consumes bitumen, honey, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and powdered iron heated in fire.
One who subsists on milk should lick these in sequence— copper, *śyāmā*, *snuhī*, *dantī*, *pathyā*, and *nepālaka*— for their juice quickly brings about the destruction of that [disease].
Having taken one part each of *bhū* (earth), *yava* (barley), and two parts of *agni* (ginger), one should drink it with warm water;
this destroys the eight types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*), especially dropsy (*jalodara*).
Milk, conch-shell, and cowrie-shells, equal in measure to the sun (turmeric) and combined with fresh butter, destroy flatulence, abdominal tumors, and colic; it is a sun to the darkness of the belly.
Śaṅkhabhāskara, which destroys all types of colic, should be consumed in a dose of half a ṭaṅka;
likewise, purified mercury and sulphur should be taken in one and two parts respectively.
One should process [the mercury] equal in weight to copper with the juices of *ārdraka* twenty-one times;
having formed a ball and sealed it in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*), one should cook it in a *gajapuṭa* fire.
One *guñjā* of ginger with ghee, followed by cold water and sugar, will quickly destroy the three *doṣas*; one should then employ cooling treatments.
It makes the thick thin and the thin thick, and kindles the digestive fire;
it treats blood fallen due to the three *doṣas*, as well as that arising from wounds, fistulas, or trauma. (Rsk 4.41)
The elixir known as *raktāri* purifies the blood arising from the liver and spleen, as well as that blood which causes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*),
and it cleanses corrupted blood.
One should grind *bola* with the juice of the sunflower for three days;
taking a single *valla* of this to be licked with honey quickly dispels obesity.
Then one should drink two palas of honey with cold water as an after-drink;
while on this *vaḍavāgni-rasa* diet, one should consume wholesome foods such as curd and avoid substances that increase *śleṣman*.

One should grind mercury, copper, and sulfur for one day with the juice of *nirguṇḍikā*, then cook it for one *yāma* in a *vālukāyantra*; this [medicine] should be administered in a dose of two *guñjās*.
One should subsequently drink a decoction of *bījapūra* roots with sugar;
this "Trivikrama" elixir cures dysuria, urinary retention, and calculi.
Having husked twenty palas of *vākucī* seeds,
one should place them in cow's urine for three weeks, along with iron and two palas of *pathyā*.
Having taken [the powder], one should dry it in the extremely harsh heat of the sun using cow's urine,
and then [place it] twenty-one times in a decoction of the bark of the *kākodumbarikā* and the *droṇa* tree.
One should prepare the mercury from the fragrance in equal measure with that powder;
having made a kajjalī with an acid, one should combine everything together in one place.
Having performed the infusion for three days with the juice of the root of the *śigru* tree and with a leaf of the *nāgavallī* plant, prepare pills weighing half a *karṣa*.
One should eat one [pill] each morning for the alleviation of white leprosy;
it is best to take the powder of the root-bark of *citraka* at night with cow’s milk.
Then, having stirred it thoroughly, one should add the finest buttermilk;
and into that one *kuḍava* measure of buttermilk, one should place eight *vallas* of sulphur in the middle.
Afterward, one should swallow two or three pills and apply an ointment of fresh butter; then, one should remain in the sun.
In one afflicted with all-white leprosy, eruptions arise like those burnt by fire;
ripening occurs in the first week, and then again in the second.
Indeed, they attain growth in the third [stage] without a doubt;
an ointment of saffron mixed with the juice of the lime fruit is beneficial.
Alternatively, a pill made of *satakrā* is beneficial when applied as an ointment with mercury;
it brings about the healing of vitiligo, becoming exceedingly beautiful and bestowing a fine complexion.
For the first seven days, buttermilk with rice should be given three times a day;
once the second seven-day period has begun, even chickpeas and dry foods may be given.
In the third week, makuṣṭha, triphalā, and ghee should be administered;
a small amount of ghee should be given, and the sufferer of white leprosy (śvitrakuṣṭhī) shall become excellent.
Endowed with prosperity, a man shall properly obtain on the surface of the earth an excellent body, radiant like a campaka flower, full of luster, and free from disease.
By the power of the king of essences (rasarāja), this is truly, truly so and not otherwise:
purified mercury, dead iron, realgar, sulfur,
antimony, harītakī, agnimantha, nirguṇḍī, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), borax, and poison.

One should grind equal parts [of the ingredients] in a mortar for one day with the juice of *nirguṇḍikā*, and for one day with the juice of *muṇḍī*; then, having formed it into pills the size of a single *guñjā* seed—
One afflicted by wind diseases should consume the *rasa* of Svacchandabhairava,
followed by a light decoction of the plant called *rāsnā* with honey as an after-drink.
Then, one should rub purified mercury for three days with decoctions of *vacā*;
likewise, one should add sulfur that has been rubbed with the juice of *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
One should knead cow’s urine into a ball and seal it within a crucible;
having coated it seven times with clay and cloth, it should be fired in a *puṭa* and then allowed to cool naturally.
One should administer four *vallās* of powdered mustard seeds as a nasal drop (*nasya*),
followed by old ghee as an after-drink (*anupāna*), using mustard oil for the oily treatment (*sneha*).
One should have an oil massage performed with that for twenty-one days;
indeed, this "Lion among the Elephants of Insanity" destroys madness and epilepsy.
One should melt mercury, fragrance, iron, and copper— one, two, one and a half, and half a *pala* respectively— in an iron vessel and pour it onto castor leaves.
Having ground it and strained it through cloth, one should cook it again in an iron vessel;
one should then add a vessel-measure of the juice of either citron or pomegranate.
Having ground it with decoctions of the five-kola group and with amlavetasa,
one should indeed administer fifty saturations (bhāvanās) thereafter.
One should add powdered roasted ṭaṅkaṇa equal in amount to all [the other ingredients];
one should add half as much viḍa as the ṭaṅkaṇa, and black pepper equal in amount to the viḍa.
Having soaked it seven times in water containing the alkaline salt of chickpeas,
one should take two or four *vallīs* of this perfected elixir.
A wise person should drink one *māṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*) and two *māṣas* of cumin (*jīraka*), combined with buttermilk (*takra*), as a post-medicinal draught (*anupāna*).
One should feed the guru meat-based food until he is full to his throat;
what is thus eaten is quickly digested, and he desires to eat again.
He is served by Ghaṭa, Śrava, Indra, Bhīma, Kumbhayoni, Caturmukha,
Śanaiścara, Rudra, and Brahmā, for the sake of Agni.
Through the cultivation of this [fire], all these have become great consumers;
therefore, it is cultivated by kings for the sake of increasing their great power.

This elixir named Kravyāda produces a marvelous digestive fire, digests food, eradicates malignant diseases, and destroys abdominal obesity; it is a destroyer of poison, a remover of the pain of colic, and a crusher of tumors and splenic disorders; it annihilates many ailments, acts as a laxative, and eliminates wind-knots and enlargement of the abdomen.
Bhairavānanda gave [the work] to Siṃhaṇa, the protector of the earth who was fond of abundant food; the king then granted him eight villages.

Sūta, bhujaṅgama, amṛta, salt, haridrā, vyoṣa, the root of dhananjaya, vanibhū, and dhātrī—these eighteen, two, nine, three, and four in number—along with śobhāñjana, fresh ginger, karīraka, and bījapūra; Rsk_4.78
Having soaked it with the juices of citron, *phaṇīśvara* creeper, and *supalāśa*, one should dry it, grind it into a powder in a mortar, and strain it through cloth;
this destroys all groups of wind disorders, as well as impaired digestion, loss of appetite, colic, and vomiting. (Rsk 4.79)
Mercury, sulphur, poison, conch-shell, cowrie-shell, borax,
and black pepper are measured in portions of one, one, three, eight, eight, three, and two respectively.
Having ground it with citron (jambīraka), it becomes Agnikumāraka;
it is used for wind disorders, weak digestion, indigestion, fever, phlegm, and cholera.
A dose the size of a *guñjā* seed should be administered in cases of seizure involving feces, urine, or the head;
it should be employed for cough, asthma, consumption, pain, and indeed for all diseases.
One should grind together three things— human ash, rock crystal, and solar salt—
and cast them into a firm, auspicious earthen pit measuring one cubit in depth.
One should place it into a well fashioned from a hollowed-out coconut shell,
and afterwards, one should wrap that joint seven times with cloth and clay.
In a shallow pan filled with sand,
having placed a horizontal medicinal pit halfway into the apparatus, one should proceed here according to the oral tradition of the venerable Guru.
Having placed the second [crucible] face down,
turned away from the furnace, one should forcibly ignite a fire beneath it until the mercury flows out.
Then, one should place the juice that causes the conch to dissolve into a glass vessel;
thereafter, one should consume one *śāṇa* of it, avoiding contact with the teeth.
This indeed bestows strength and nourishment; it destroys abdominal tumors, enlargement of the spleen or liver, abscesses, glandular swellings, and colic, and it digests consumed food in an instant.
Behold, oh world, the wonderful majesty of mercury:
for when copper, water, and iron are cast into it, they indeed melt away.
Having added mercury and one-third part of sulfur,
one should grind them together with a tenth part of navasāra and the juice of the unmadaka plant.
Having ground all of that together in a mortar,
one should place it inside a glass flask situated within a sand-bath (vālukāyantra) according to the tradition taught by the Guru.
One should cook it for sixteen watches (yāmas) with mild, medium, and intense fire;
once cooked and thoroughly cooled, it should be taken, and it becomes the *haragaurī-rasa*.
Having made equal parts of mercury and sulfur, they should be rubbed with the milk of *sarpākṣī* and cooked as before; others, however, know this to be the essence of Hara and Gaurī.
Having added twice the amount of mercury to sulphur and processed it with the juices of cotton plants as before, this is known as the Kāmadeva-rasa.
Equal parts of gold, silver, and copper should be cast together and ground for three days with *musalī*, *akhuparṇī*, and the juice of *mātuluṅga*.
Then, the mercury that conquers death (*mṛtyuñjaya-rasa*) is prepared with *mocaka*, *ciñcā*, and *ātmaguptā*.
The consumption of these three is said to be wholesome; their qualities are realized gradually.
It should always be consumed for one month by the best of men along with sugar and clarified butter.
Having thus practiced with the lord of elixirs (sūtendra), one should always eat sweet food:
śāli rice, cow’s milk, sugar-candy, white sugar, and the meat of wild animals.
Preparations made from wheat, black gram, rice, plantains,
jackfruit, dates, grapes, and coconut.
A wise person should consume everything that is said to be aphrodisiac;
it destroys wrinkles after one year and gray hair after two years.
Through service, his body becomes adamantine; by means of the melting of the two, he attains a hundred Nītās.
There is no depletion of his semen; even a eunuch acts like a man.
With his *liṅga* perpetually erect, he shall attain the imperishable state of Lalanā;
possessing a complexion like the color of molten gold, he will be adorned with prosperity, wisdom, and intelligence.
Hayavega, Mayūrākṣa, and Vārāhaśruti;
and another, Kāmadeva, who crushes the pride of the haughty woman.
It destroys diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā), urinary disorders (meha), chronic fevers (jīrṇajvara),
malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), diarrhea (atīsāra), and excessive urination (bahumūtra) caused by cow's buttermilk.
Indeed, this elixir named Mṛtyuñjaya— the essence of Hara, Gaurī, and Kāmadeva— removes all diseases when taken with its own appropriate medicinal adjuncts.
What is the use of much speaking here? There are three [remedies] that remove old age and death:
one should consume two *vallās* of *kajjalī* made from equal parts of mercury (*sūta*) and sulfur (*gandha*), along with the seeds of *unmatta*, rubbed with its oil, together with sugar and milk.
It destroys the flood of urine, increases virility, and causes the woman to flow;
this elixir bestows desire upon men and crushes the pride of haughty women.
Gold-seed, poison, mercury-ore, and haṃsapāda are for the process of *jāraṇa*.
Pure mercury should be steamed for three days over a mild fire in buffalo curd;
as it breaks apart, more curd should be added, and on the fourth day, one should extract it.
Into that, the wise one should throw gold weighing one sixty-fourth part;
he should grind it with lime juice until indeed a single unity is produced.
Furthermore, by again steaming that mercury with the juices of *vaṭa* shoots,
*ahivallī*, *kākamācī*, and *jīvantī*, it will be freed from the pair of diseases.
For one day it should remain in a pitcher of cold water, and for one day in buffalo curd;
thus, observing celibacy, one should take one *valla* of the perfected elixir every day.
For one month, the husband should consume white sugar, milk, and boiled rice as his preferred diet;
meanwhile, the woman should take the juices of *triphalā*, *nimba*, and *kārpāsī* separately, in successive order.
Having drunk [the juice] for seven days at the onset of the season,
one should take one *valla* of the essence for three days, combined with cotton-seed water and sugar.
A paste of borax, rock crystal, and mercury,
combined with the juice of ripe tamarind and applied to the vagina with honey for three days, is an excellent means of purification.
At the time of serving women, during the night, one should consume three *māṣaka* of mercury extracted during the day and placed in the midst of curd, combined with curd, as prescribed by Mahiṣī.
At the end of the enjoyment, one should likewise remain for half a watch in union;
thus, one gives birth to an excellent son endowed with all auspicious marks.
When heat and other such symptoms have arisen, the physician should always administer grapes, sugar, and the like, and prescribe cooling treatments for the young woman.
Created by Rudra, this [mantra] bestows an increase in lifespan, strength, and luster; it enhances lost virility, removes disease, and grants sons.
One part of mercury, one part of nāgāñjana, and one and a half parts of silver,
finely ground into powder— this collyrium for the eyes produces divine vision.

One should purify the mercury and the fragrance equally, and then process them seven times in succession with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, and with the juices of the two types of *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *pathyā*, and *ubhayā*.
Equal parts of powdered *nepālaja* (realgar) should be mixed together and ground;
two *valla*s of this should be administered with warm water along with eight times the amount of jaggery (*guḍa*).
First the impurities, then the water, and thereafter the undigested matter gradually; everything that is foul exits from the abdomen along with the intestines.
Once purgation has occurred and one is thoroughly cleansed, the wholesome diet of curd and rice is beneficial;
the *sāraṇasundara* elixir will conquer diseases such as fever and others.
One part each of mercury (rāḍha), copper (arka), and madhuka, along with one and a half parts and two and five parts [respectively],
and one ṭaṅka of water added— this is known as the Vāmaka rasa.
One should grind equal parts of mercury, sulfur, and the three pungents (vyoṣa) with *unmattaka* for a day;
this elixir named *Unmatta* is an errhine (*nasya*) that conquers *sannipāta*.
Copper leaf smeared with fragrance, heated in fire and then beaten,
its powder combined with buttermilk in a dose of half a *valla* will cause intense vomiting.
Crystal, tuttha, nepāla, black pepper, neem seeds,
and the marrow of putrajīvaka, [mixed] with lime juice in a vessel of arka wood.
One should administer seven pills, each the size of a *guñjā* seed, as a collyrium;
this will destroy *sannipāta*, epilepsy, and snake venom.
Black *ākallaka* poison and the ash of the fruit of the *hemadru* tree,
when used as a dusting powder in proportions of one, two, three, or eight parts, remove perspiration.

A pill composed of poison (*viṣa*), the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), turmeric (*haridrā*), *musta* grass (*abda*), neem leaves (*nimbapatra*), and *viḍaṅga*, bound together with goat’s urine, is the victorious *jayā*, the carrier of medicinal properties (*yogavāhikā*). (Rsk 5.1)
The poison of *sūta* (mercury) and *arka*, *gandha*, *viḍaṅga*, *agni*, *abja*, *kesara*, *reṇukā*, *granthika*, and *bola*;
for all these, there should be double the amount of jaggery (*guḍa*). *Rṣikulyā 5.2*
One should indeed consume a pill the size of a jujube fruit in the early morning for cough,
asthma, consumption, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and irregular fever.
In cases of grief, anemia, leprosy, malabsorption syndrome, hemorrhoids, and fistula-in-ano,
this Vijayā pill, proclaimed by Rudra, is indeed superior in its qualities.
Take *aṅkola*, fire (citraka), fragrance (musta), black pepper, mercury, poison, and bile (guggulu) in successive order; add sea salt and process them with three applications of *arka* milk.

Then, having ground the mixture with neem water, form pills the size of a *guñjā* seed. One should administer this pill named Śaṅkarā—measured by the sequence five, five, six, ten, three, five, and ten—to cure phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, fever, abdominal disease, and consumption.

One pala each of ciñcā, kṣāra, and paṭu, along with a vraja (salt), should be ground into a paste with lime juice. Into that, one pala of conch shell, heated repeatedly, should be quenched until it is completely reduced to powder.

Then, having added one pala each of hiṅgu, vyoṣa, rasā, amṛta, and bālaka—each weighing one niṣka—one should form pills the size of a conch-shell fragment. This Śaṅkhavaṭī conquers consumption, grahaṇī, abdominal tumors, and colic.
Take equal parts of *rasa* (emetic nut), black *abhayā*, *tvakṣa*, *vāsā*, and *bhārgī*, each increasing in quantity by one step;
to this add an equal amount of the heartwood of *khadira*, all of which has been saturated with a decoction of *babbūla*.
This pill, measured at one akṣa and prepared with honey twenty-one times, destroys cough, dyspnea, consumption, and hiccup; it is known as Kāsakartarī, the "Cutter of Cough."

A wick made from equal parts of *vyoṣa*, *granthi*, *vacā*, *agni*, *hiṅgu*, the two *jaraṇas*, *viṣa*, *nimbuka*, and *ārdraka*—all ground together with *asava*—is called *Sūryaprabhā*. When applied, it destroys all colic and wind disorders throughout the entire body, and it quickly kindles the digestive fire like that of Vāḍava. (Rsk 5.9)
Cardamom, camphor, sugar, emblic myrobalan, nutmeg, silk-cotton tree, and gokṣura—
along with the ashes of mercury, tin, and iron— all these should be taken in equal parts and thoroughly infused.

Then, one half-pala measure of *guḍūcī* and *śālmalikā* decoctions, combined with honey, should be formed into pills known as "Candrakalā"; these are to be administered in all types of urinary disorders (*meha*).
Cinnabar, the four spices (caturjāta), cloves, medicinal herbs, sandalwood, nutmeg, saffron, black pepper, ākalla, and opium.
All [the ingredients] should be equal to musk and camphor;
with honey, a pill the size of a jujube fruit (*kola*) should be made, known as *Bhogapurandari*.
For this indeed causes the retention of semen, increases strength and flesh,
and enables a man, with steady organs, to go [in union] a hundred times like a sparrow.
A pill named after Nāgārjuna, consisting of tin, green vitriol, and black iron sulphide in equal parts with guñjā, taken with fresh ginger water, destroys diseases caused by phlegm and wind.

Take eight parts each of triphalā, viḍaṅga, soma, bhallātaka, vahi, and viśvā; there should be eight parts of white vacā and one part of dhattūra (sadviṣa). All of this, ground with cow’s urine, should be made into pills the size of chickpeas.
The wise should administer the shade-dried [substance] in the sequence of three, two, one, and four [units].
Even a man suffering from snake venom, cholera, or a mallet-like affliction, or one afflicted by malignant indigestion or the three humors (tridoṣa),
shall live immediately— even if already dead— by the power of this pill.
A pill prepared from the root, leaf, or fruit of the plant born of *kitava*,
combined with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), instantly destroys wind disorders corrupted by the three humors along with insanity.
A pill weighing one *śāṇa* should be made from *kaṭphala*, water, *gila*, *kṛṣṇā*, *hiṅgula*, *bola*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, mixed with jaggery; on the ninth day, [this is administered].
It should be administered with warm water; it immediately removes the poison of a rabid dog.
Alternatively, a powder of *garabhr̥ṅga* and *uṣaṇa*, taken with clarified butter, destroys that same poison.
One should prepare pills the size of chickpeas, enriched with the juices of the two types of *brāhmī*, along with mercury, copper, sulfur, *suratiktā*, yellow *bhṛṅga*, and black pepper.
One [mudrā] should first be given to one who is deficient in the three humors, even if he has fainted;
another after a moment; another after a watch (prahara); and no other at all.
Even a man who is dead lives again when afflicted by the lassitude born of the three humors;
this is the pill known as the "Reviver of the Dead," proclaimed by the illustrious Nāgārjuna. (Rsk 5.23)
A pill made from elavāluka, bhayābola, indrā, and guggulu,
combined with the milky sap of snuhī, cures swelling and destroys fever.
Excellent trikaṭu, the best tuttha, yaṣṭī, vella, arka,
vārija, rodhra, and rasāñjana— these should be made into a powder and formed into a wick with rainwater.
It immediately cures inflammation of the eyes with breast milk, cataracts with water decocted from *rodhra*,
and it destroys blood-redness with the juice of *kiṃśuka* as well as the flower of *villa*.
A leaf of the *pāṭala* tree [written] with goat’s urine [is used] for paralyzing or causing the falling down of walls;
this was written by Nāgārjuna and removes all diseases of the eyes.
Vyoṣa, varā, excellent hiṅgu, tikta, ugrā, naktamālaka, and gaurī—these pungent substances, dried in the shade and made into pills with goat’s urine, [are effective]. (Rsk 5.28)
It destroys epilepsy, loss of memory, insanity, headache,
night-blindness, cataracts, disorders caused by spirits and the like, and dizziness.
Through immersion, one should destroy the fevers known as the first, second, third, and fourth,
as well as the loss of consciousness caused by *sannipāta*, thereby restoring clear awareness.
Vajrī milk processed with fire and combined with rock salt,
when drunk in a dose of two *valla*s with warm water, causes purgation and destroys fever.
Salt that has been saturated once with the milk of a cow exposed to the sun,
when drunk in a dose of half a karṣa along with cow’s milk, induces vomiting.

One should grind equal parts of mercury, sulphur, yellow orpiment, and realgar in a mortar with *sauvīra* (sour gruel) for one day; with that mixture, one should smear a cloth and form it into a wick.
After repeatedly anointing it with oil, one should then ignite a fire. From that, the black oil which has dripped down should be used as an ointment for the body.
One shall conquer all tremors of the calves, arms, hands, feet, and head; leprosy, severe fistula-in-ano, clusters of ulcers, diseases, and great sciatica (mahāgṛdhrasī);
other groups of diseases born of wind (vāta), and difficult-to-cure sinus ulcers. This is the renowned Great Vātāri-taila, the remover of ailments throughout the three worlds. (Rsk 5.34)
Asafoetida, neem leaves, and sea-foam—
these should be taken in equal parts, and likewise, white poison (white arsenic) should be added.
One should cook pungent oil combined with cow urine;
with that very [oil], one should fill the ears of men, elephants, and horses.
This oil, named Karṇāmṛta, created by Brahmā himself, quickly destroys diseases of the ear and ailments of the head through its application as an ointment.
Musk, camphor, bāhlīka, nakha, māṃsī, sarjaka, mustā, aguru, and sugar— all these, increasing in quantity by one unit each, are equal to the amount of saffron.
One should drop oil little by little for one day and then grind it;
having extinguished a burning wick, it emits a divine smoke.
Beloved by all the gods, this incense— bestowing the accomplishment of all mantras—
is dear to kings when used for bathing, clothing, and the bedchamber.
It was prepared by Cāmuṇḍa in Yoginīpura in the year measured by the earth, fire, and lunar days (131).
He composed the *Rasasaṃketakalikā*, which bestows the attainment of one's desired goals.
